Beállítom Összesen kb. 40 milliárd forintnyi összeget fordított az előző kormányzat arra, hogy különböző külföldi országokban ingatlanokat vásároljon – tudta meg a Hvg.hu közérdekű adatigénylés nyomán. A Magyar Nemzeti Vagyonkezelőtől érkező információk szerint a fenti összegért 26 ingatlan tulajdonjoga került a magyar államhoz, amely ezeket is ideértve jelenleg – a 2010 előtt vásárolt ingatlanokat is figyelembe véve – összesen 158 olyan ingatlant birtokol, amely valamilyen hivatalos munkának biztosít helyet. A legtöbbet a 2021-ben vásárolt Londoni Magyar Házra fizetett ki az állam: a Cockspur Street 17–19. szám alatti épület, mely negyedórára fekszik a Buckingham-palotától és a Westminster-palotától, 9,5 milliárd forintért került állami tulajdonba. A ház 1907-ben épült Sir Aston Webb tervei alapján – neki köszönhető pl. a Buckingham-palota mai kinézete is –, hogy a kanadai Grand Trunk Railway vasúttársaság londoni székháza legyen. Bővebben itt írtunk az épületről . A második legtöbbet a Németországban, Münchenben található, főkonzulátusnak helyet biztosító épületért kellett kifizetni, ez 6 milliárd forintjába került az államnak 2019-ben, míg a Brüsszelben található Magyarország Ház volt a harmadik legdrágább, amiért 3,5 milliárd forintot fizetett ki az előző kormányzat 2021-ben. Az előző kormányzati kiadásokról folyamatosan érkeznek a hírek. Pár napja szintén a Hvg.hu számolt be arról, hogy Szijjártó Péter és az őt kísérő stáb több mint 51 millió forintot költött külföldi VIP-várókra a repülőgépes utak során. https://www.dw.com/en/ukraine-poland-say.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5MWuq No casualties were reported following the drone strikes near Poland Image: Sylwester Uchanski/REUTERS Advertisement Russia launched two drone strikes on western Ukraine, very near its border with NATO member Poland , Ukrainian and Polish authorities said on Sunday. One of the drones hit a passenger train locomotive in Volyn, some two kilometers (1.24 miles) from the border crossing. "The monitoring team gave the train crew advanced warning, and thanks to that, no one was injured," Ukrainian railway operator Ukrzaliznytsia said in online post. Putin rejects Zelenskyy's G20 talks offer To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The company later said that a "systemic attack" was happening throughout Ukraine. Separately, Poland's PKP Intercity confirmed that they have taken control of the affected train following the attack in the Ukrainian territory . "The train is carrying 206 people. There are no Polish citizens among the passengers," the operator said online. "After completing customs clearance, it will continue its journey towards Warsaw." Zelenskyy: Locomotive 'deliberately burned' On Sunday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the locomotive was "deliberately burned" and a gas station damaged in Volyn. "It is precisely to prevent these strikes from spreading further into Europe that Ukrainian men and women fight every day, give their lives, and do not allow the aggression to expand," he said. Moscow did not immediately comment on the reports. Falling debris set a gas station on fire near the border checkpoint in Volyn Image: Sylwester Uchanski/REUTERS Ukrainian officials also reported another drone strike on Yahodyn overnight, some half a mile (800 meters) from the Polish border. The border with Poland serves as essential transit point for military and humanitarian aid. 'Putin's terror 'knocking' directly on the doors' — Ukrainian foreign minister Commenting on the Yahodyn incident, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the "barbaric" attacks were more than "just a continuation of its attacks on our state borders." "This is Putin's terror 'knocking' directly on the doors of the EU and NATO. Russian barbarians are at your gate, dear partners," he said in an English-language post on X. He urged Ukraine's Western allies to make Russia "feel the consequences of its terror. Not just half-decisions, but uncompromising, powerful steps. Full trade embargo. Full entry bans. Full sanctions on the military-industrial complex." "Putin needs to understand that his barbarism will be met with decisive action that increases the cost of war for him to an unacceptable level," he added. Image: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement US President Donald Trump has called concerns that artificial intelligence is progressing too quickly a "SICK conspiracy." Trump's statement followed calls by tech leaders such as Anthropic's Dario Amodei and OpenAI 's Sam Altman for more governmental regulation of AI. In recent months, several incidents have highlighted the risk that AI agents could go rogue. What Trump said about AI 'guardrails' "The only control or ‘guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!" Trump posted on his Truth Social account. Anthropic is the developer of the popular AI model Claude Image: IMAGO/ZUMA Press Trump added that his administration has already prevented Anthropic from "doing bad, or potentially bad" things with the technology. The Pentagon previously tried to brand Anthropic's models a security risk and posed a temporary ban on one of its more advanced models. "There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China," Trump wrote. Anthropic boss Amodei warned against uncontrolled global AI development over the weekend saying that there's a risk of AI-led agents taking over the entire internet within six to 12 months. Microsoft published its own code of conduct to ensure human control over AI. This led to AI stocks falling worldwide, including those of chip maker Nvidia (3.5%) and Elon Musk 's SpaceX (1.7%). https://www.ibtimes.co.uk/ukraine-starsh.text: Ukrainian defence forces reported speed limits on military-grade Starshield satellite terminals operating across Ukraine overnight from 13 to 14 October. They claim the change disrupted drone operations as relations between Kyiv and Washington deteriorated.The terminals lose satellite connectivity when travelling faster than 100mp/h (160km/h). Ukrainian officials alleged the restriction was politically motivated.US officials denied involvement in the restrictions, while SpaceX Chief Executive Elon Musk stated on X that Starshield operational parameters are set directly by the US Department of Defense rather than commercial SpaceX policy.Drone Operations Disrupted Without WarningUkrainian forces said the new speed restrictions on Starshield terminals disrupted telemetry for high-speed interceptor drones used to counter Russian jet-powered Shahed drones. Mid-range strike drones, frontline reconnaissance and tactical logistics were also affected.Starshield is SpaceX's separate, military-grade satellite network, funded by the US Department of Defense. According to Musk, its operating rules, including speed limits, are set by the US military and government.In Ukraine, encrypted Starshield terminals help keep drones, frontline units and logistics connected, including in areas where radio communications are jammed. Field units reported data links dropping for 10 to 20 seconds at high speeds or disappearing entirely.Serhii Beskrestnov, a military technology adviser to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said Ukrainian forces received no advance warning of the speed ceiling. He said it caused several active combat missions to fail or be cancelled. Units including the 7th Air Assault Corps in the Huliaipole sector reportedly aborted supply and surveillance operations.Responding to criticism on X, SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk said Starshield was a government system funded through US Department of Defense contracts. He distinguished it from commercial Starlink, which he said was intended strictly for civilian or defensive use.Mykhailo Fedorov, a former Ukrainian defence minister, said connectivity had been partially restored, although the 160km/h speed threshold remained. Ukrainian authorities said removing the restriction entirely was essential to maintaining the country's air defences.Dispute Escalates Over Ukrainian Strikes on Russian RefineriesTrump had publicly criticised Zelenskyy over Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries, blaming them for higher global fuel prices. He also suggested Ukraine should elect a new president.Reports said senior US officials warned Kyiv that access to US intelligence sharing and channels for purchasing Patriot interceptors could be suspended if attacks on Russian energy infrastructure continued. Trump and Matthew Whitaker, the US ambassador to NATO, publicly denied that intelligence cooperation had been halted.Before the slowdown, the Trump administration had eased sanctions on Russian fuel under a diesel supply arrangement with Moscow and declared a unilateral energy ceasefire. Zelenskyy accused Russia of violating the truce with continued missile attacks on Ukrainian energy facilities.In an interview, Zelenskyy said he felt betrayed by Washington's shift. He said restricting satellite communications weakened air defences and cost lives, adding that those responsible understood the consequences. His account differed from statements by SpaceX and US officials.Europe Looks for Ways to Strengthen Ukraine's Air DefencesPolish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski questioned on social media whether satellite services were being used as geopolitical leverage, saying European customers were watching contractor reliability.British leaders agreed to accelerate air defence support for Kyiv, bringing forward £10 million worth of Lightweight Multirole Missiles from a £45-million package intended to counter jet-powered drones.European partners also approved a military space programme involving up to €24 billion (£20 billion) in investmentand a joint orbital data-sharing agreement. Alternatives under evaluation include the European Union's IRIS² constellation, national military networks and providers such as Eutelsat.
